## What Changed

**`src/time.js`** — `dayKey` no longer slices the first 10 characters of the timestamp. It now:

- Parses the ISO 8601 timestamp, including `Z`, `±HH:MM`, and `±HHMM` offsets.
- Converts the instant to IST (`UTC+05:30`) before extracting the calendar date.
- Handles date-only values, optional seconds/fractional seconds, leap days, month/year rollover, and `24:00:00`.
- Rejects invalid dates instead of silently normalizing them.
- Is independent of the host machine's timezone.
- Treats timestamps without an explicit offset as UTC.

**`src/report.js`** — unchanged; it already delegates day calculation to `dayKey`.

## Evidence

Before the fix, the reproducer failed the 18:30Z boundary and offset cases:

```
FAIL 2026-11-02T20:30:00Z -> 2026-11-02 (want 2026-11-03)
FAIL 2026-11-02T18:30:00Z -> 2026-11-02 (want 2026-11-03)
FAIL 2026-11-02T23:30:00-08:00 -> 2026-11-02 (want 2026-11-03)
FAIL 2025-12-31T19:00:00Z -> 2025-12-31 (want 2026-01-01)
```

After the fix, all checks passed:

- 18:29:59Z → `2026-11-02`; 18:30:00Z → `2026-11-03`
- `+05:30`, `-08:00`, `-05:00`, `+0530`, `Z`, and `z` offsets
- Year rollover, leap day, date-only, `24:00:00`, fractional seconds
- 8 invalid-input cases correctly throw
- `ordersPerDay` integration: 4 orders bucketed as `{ "2026-11-03": 3, "2026-11-02": 1 }`

The root cause was using the UTC date prefix (`iso.slice(0, 10)`) as the report day. Orders between 18:30Z and 23:59Z belong to the next IST calendar day, so those late-night orders were counted on the wrong date. The fix converts the actual instant into IST before extracting the day, at the source in `dayKey`.

## What Changed

`src/invoice.js` — GST is now calculated once on the invoice’s total taxable amount instead of per line:

```js
let taxable = 0
for (const line of lines) {
  taxable += lineTotal(line)
}
const gst = gstOn(taxable, ratePercent)
return { taxable, gst, total: taxable + gst }
```

## Root Cause

The old implementation called `gstOn` for every line and summed the individually rounded GST amounts. Each line was rounded to the nearest paisa, so the accumulated rounding error could differ from the accountant’s single rounding of GST on the whole taxable amount.

Reproduction before the fix — three 1-paise lines at 18%:

```text
actual   { taxable: 3, gst: 0, total: 3 }
expected { taxable: 3, gst: 1, total: 4 }
```

## Evidence

After the fix, all checks passed:

```text
PASS three 1-paise lines @18% { taxable: 3, gst: 1, total: 4 }
PASS mixed lines @18% { taxable: 648, gst: 117, total: 765 }
PASS single line @5% { taxable: 999, gst: 50, total: 1049 }
PASS empty invoice { taxable: 0, gst: 0, total: 0 }
```

`tax.js`’s half-up rounding remains unchanged; only the point at which rounding is applied was corrected.

## Why

Rounding once at the invoice level matches the accountant’s calculation and eliminates paisa discrepancies caused by summing per-line rounded GST amounts.

```js
export function truncate(text, n) {

  return text.length > limit ? text.slice(0, limit - 1) + "…" : text
}
```

## What Changed

- `src/settings.js`
  - Added single-flight loading so concurrent cold-cache reads share one `db.all()` call.
  - Added a generation counter so a load that started before a save cannot install its stale snapshot into the cache.
  - Added `invalidateSettings()` to clear the cache and any in-flight load reference.
- `src/admin.js`
  - `saveSetting()` now invalidates the settings cache immediately after the write completes.

## Evidence

All three scenarios pass:

```text
PASS: cold burst deduped; save invalidates immediately
PASS: stale in-flight load cannot bring old value back
PASS: stale load does not poison cache after it resolves
```

Verified:
- 20 concurrent cold reads → `db.loads() === 1`.
- Save followed by read → new value returned, with exactly one reload.
- Read started before a save → stale snapshot cannot repopulate the cache; subsequent reads see the new value.

## Why

The original cache had no write-path invalidation, so reads could stay stale for the full 60-second TTL. It also had no in-flight deduplication, causing a cold-cache stampede. The generation check closes the race where a slow load finishes after a save and overwrites the cache with the old snapshot.

Note: a read that began before a save may still resolve with the snapshot it already requested, but that snapshot is never cached again.
